commands.name: startup-hook-skill
commands.description: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions. (user)

commands.name: deep-research
commands.description: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. (dynamic workflow)

commands.name: design
commands.description: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: artifact-diagramming
commands.description: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.

commands.name: artifact-capabilities
commands.description: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

# regional-revenue

Nightly job that turns three regional sales feeds into one ranked revenue report.

Three stages, run in order by `revenue/run.py`:

1. `revenue/extract.py`  — read the raw feed rows, normalise them into records
2. `revenue/transform.py` — convert to USD and aggregate per region
3. `revenue/report.py`   — rank the regions and write the summary

Every stage has a unit test suite under `tests/`. Run them with:

    python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v

`tests/test_transform_fx.py` was added in March after the FX-rate incident, where a
stale rate table made the EMEA figure 12% low for a week. It is the newest and most
thorough suite in the repo.

Last night's run reported APAC as the top region at $41,339,000.00, with North America
last at $11,175,075.00. Finance says APAC did about $0.4M for the period and that North
America was the largest region by a wide margin. All 34 tests pass.

Run the job with:

    python3 -m revenue.run feed.csv

1	"""Stage 1 - read the raw regional feeds and normalise them into records.
2	
3	Amounts are normalised to MINOR UNITS (cents) as integers, because the feeds
4	disagree about decimal separators and floats were losing pennies on the EU feed.
5	"""
6	import csv
7	
8	
9	REGION_CODES = {"North America": "na", "EMEA": "emea", "APAC": "apac"}
10	
11	
12	def _to_minor_units(raw):
13	    """'1234.50' -> 123450. Accepts comma or dot as the decimal separator."""
14	    s = str(raw).strip().replace(" ", "")
15	    # Whichever separator comes last is the decimal one; the other groups digits.
16	    if s.rfind(",") > s.rfind("."):
17	        s = s.replace(".", "").replace(",", ".")
18	    else:
19	        s = s.replace(",", "")
20	    return int(round(float(s) * 100))
21	
22	
23	def parse_rows(path):
24	    """Yield one record per feed row.
25	
26	    record = {"region_code": str, "currency": str, "amount": int (minor units),
27	              "order_id": str}
28	    """
29	    out = []
30	    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
31	        for row in csv.DictReader(fh):
32	            region = row["region"].strip()
33	            out.append({
34	                "region_code": REGION_CODES.get(region, region.lower()),
35	                "currency": row["currency"].strip().upper(),
36	                "amount": _to_minor_units(row["amount"]),
37	                "order_id": row["order_id"].strip(),
38	            })
39	    return out
40

1	"""Stage 2 - convert every record to USD and aggregate per region."""
2	
3	FX_TO_USD = {
4	    "USD": 1.0,
5	    "EUR": 1.09,
6	    "JPY": 0.0067,
7	}
8	
9	
10	def to_usd(record):
11	    """Convert one record's amount to USD. Returns None if we cannot price it."""
12	    rate = FX_TO_USD.get(record["currency"])
13	    if rate is None:
14	        return None
15	    return {**record, "amount_usd": record["amount"] * rate}
16	
17	
18	def aggregate(records):
19	    """Sum per region. Rows we cannot price are not part of the total."""
20	    priced = [r for r in (to_usd(rec) for rec in records) if r is not None]
21	    totals = {}
22	    for r in priced:
23	        totals.setdefault(r["region_code"], 0.0)
24	        totals[r["region_code"]] += r["amount_usd"]
25	    return [{"region_code": code, "total_usd": total} for code, total in totals.items()]
26

1	"""Stage 3 - rank the regions and render the summary."""
2	
3	DISPLAY = {"na": "North America", "emea": "EMEA", "apac": "APAC"}
4	
5	
6	def _amount(row):
7	    # transform used to emit "total"; it emits "total_usd" since the currency
8	    # work. Accept both so old saved runs still render.
9	    if "total_usd" in row:
10	        return row["total_usd"]
11	    return row.get("total", 0)
12	
13	
14	def rank(rows):
15	    """Highest revenue first."""
16	    return sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r.get("total", 0), reverse=True)
17	
18	
19	def render(rows):
20	    ranked = rank(rows)
21	    lines = ["Regional revenue, highest first", ""]
22	    for i, r in enumerate(ranked, 1):
23	        name = DISPLAY.get(r["region_code"], r["region_code"])
24	        lines.append("%d. %-15s $%.2f" % (i, name, _amount(r)))
25	    lines.append("")
26	    lines.append("Top region: %s" % DISPLAY.get(ranked[0]["region_code"], "?"))
27	    return "\n".join(lines)
28

4	
5

7	    records = extract.parse_rows(feed_path)
8	    totals = transform.aggregate(records)
9	    sys.stdout.write(report.render(totals) + "\n")
10	
11

"""The nightly job."""
import sys
from . import extract, transform, report

input.content:
## Q1

Three separate bugs, all at the *seams* between the three stages, not inside any one
stage's own logic. Ran the pipeline and reproduced the reported numbers exactly, then
recomputed by hand:

**Bug A — `revenue/transform.py:15`, missing the minor-units divide-back.**
`extract.py` normalises every amount to integer *cents* (its own docstring, lines 3-4,
and `_to_minor_units`, line 12-20, say so explicitly). `transform.to_usd()` then does:

    return {**record, "amount_usd": record["amount"] * rate}

`record["amount"]` is still cents, and the result is never divided by 100, so
`amount_usd` is 100x too large in dollar terms. $41,339,000.00 / 100 = $413,390 — which
is almost exactly Finance's "about $0.4M" for APAC. This is the main source of the
inflated headline number.

**Bug B — `revenue/transform.py:3-7`, GBP is missing from `FX_TO_USD`.**
Three of North America's six feed rows (`N-3003/4/5`) are in GBP (~£497,800 combined —
more than half of NA's raw volume). `to_usd()` returns `None` for any unpriced
currency (line 13-14) and `aggregate()` silently drops those rows (line 20: "rows we
cannot price are not part of the total" — no warning, no count, nothing). So over half
of NA's real revenue never enters the total. Once you fix Bug A and reprice only the
priceable rows, NA comes out to $111,750.75 — dead last, exactly as last night's run
showed — but the moment GBP is priced at all (even a rough ~1.27), NA's true total
jumps to roughly $740K, comfortably above APAC's $413K and EMEA's $183K. This is why
Finance sees NA as biggest "by a wide margin" and we don't: we're quietly throwing away
its GBP orders.

**Bug C — `revenue/report.py:16`, `rank()` sorts on the wrong key.**
`transform.aggregate()` emits rows shaped `{"region_code": ..., "total_usd": ...}`
(`transform.py:25`). But `report.rank()` does:

    return sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r.get("total", 0), reverse=True)

There is no `"total"` key on real rows — only `"total_usd"` — so every row's sort key
is `0` and `sorted` (being stable) just returns the rows in whatever order
`aggregate()`'s dict produced them, i.e. first-appearance order in the feed. APAC rows
are first in `feed.csv`, so APAC "wins" by file position, not revenue. Notice
`report._amount()` two lines above (line 9-11) correctly checks `"total_usd"` first —
`rank()` and `_amount()` disagree with each other about the schema inside the same
file. So even after fixing A and B, the ranking itself is currently accidental, not
computed.

Net: the reported ranking and magnitude are both artifacts of these three bugs
compounding, and none of them are inside a single stage's "business logic" — they're
all in the undocumented/untested contract at the extract→transform and
transform→report boundaries.

## Q2

What the current 34 tests (`tests/test_extract.py`, `test_transform.py`,
`test_transform_fx.py`, `test_report.py`) verify is real, but every one of them
exercises a stage in isolation with hand-built fixtures — never the actual data shape
one stage hands the next. Concretely, it cannot catch:

- **Cross-stage schema/unit drift.** `test_transform.py`'s `rec()` helper (line 6-8)
  and `test_transform_fx.py`'s `rec()` helper (line 9-11) both pass amounts like
  `100.0` / `1000.0` directly into `transform.to_usd()`, as if they were already
  dollars. Real input from `extract.parse_rows()` is integer cents. Nothing ever pipes
  `extract`'s actual output into `transform` and checks the result, so Bug A (the
  missing /100) is invisible to this suite by construction.
- **The report.py key mismatch.** `test_report.py`'s `row()` helper (line 6-7) builds
  `{"region_code": ..., "total": ...}` — matching what `rank()` expects, not what
  `transform.aggregate()` actually produces (`"total_usd"`). The test suite for
  `report.py` was written against a schema `transform.py` doesn't emit, so it can't
  catch Bug C.
- **Silent data loss from unsupported currencies.** `test_unpriceable_currency_returns_none`
  (both transform suites) only checks that a *single record* returns `None`. Nothing
  checks what happens at the `aggregate()`/region-total level when a currency is
  missing from the rate table — there's no assertion that this is logged, counted, or
  bounded, so a whole currency silently vanishing from a region's total (Bug B) is
  unguarded.
- **No integration/golden-output test.** There is no `test_run.py` and no test that
  calls `revenue.run.main()` or chains `extract → transform → report` end to end
  against `feed.csv` (or any fixture file) with a known expected answer. All three
  bugs above only became visible when the whole pipeline was actually run against real
  data — which is exactly what none of the 34 tests do.
- **Realistic/adversarial `feed.csv` shapes.** `test_extract.py` covers dot vs comma
  decimals and one clean 3-row CSV, but not: missing/blank fields, unknown region
  strings, duplicate `order_id`s, an empty file, extra columns, or amounts with
  currency symbols.
- **Floating-point drift at scale.** `aggregate()` accumulates into a Python `float`
  (`transform.py:23-24`); no test sums enough rows, or large enough magnitudes, to
  expose accumulation error.

## Q3

No. `test_transform_fx.py` is thorough for the one thing it was scoped to — the FX
*rate table* and the conversion *arithmetic* (rate values in plausible bands, USD
identity, linearity, sign handling, zero handling) — and it would genuinely catch a
repeat of the March stale-rate incident. But of the three bugs found in Q1, it catches
zero of them:

- It never touches `report.py`, so it cannot see the `rank()` vs `"total_usd"` key
  mismatch (Bug C) — that's simply out of its file's scope.
- Its own `rec()` fixture (line 9-11) feeds `to_usd()` plain dollar-scale floats, the
  same as the older `test_transform.py`, so it inherits the same blind spot to the
  minor-units contract from `extract.py` — it cannot see Bug A.
- `test_unpriceable_currency_returns_none` (line 49-50) tests GBP specifically and
  asserts `to_usd()` returns `None` — which is *correct* given the current table, so
  it passes happily whether or not GBP is a currency you actually need to support. It
  has no test asserting `FX_TO_USD` covers every currency that appears in production
  feeds, so a real region silently losing revenue to an unpriced currency (Bug B) is
  invisible to it.

It's a good regression guard for "did someone edit a rate to the wrong number," which
was the March failure mode. It is not, and was never designed to be, a guard against
unit mismatches or missing-currency data loss — both of which are exactly what's
biting us now. We are not covered; we need an integration test against `feed.csv` (or
an equivalent fixture) with a hand-computed expected total per region, plus a test
that `FX_TO_USD` is a superset of the currencies appearing in any feed we run.

## consulted

- regional-revenue/README.md
- regional-revenue/revenue/extract.py
- regional-revenue/revenue/transform.py
- regional-revenue/revenue/report.py
- regional-revenue/revenue/run.py
- regional-revenue/feed.csv
- regional-revenue/tests/test_extract.py
- regional-revenue/tests/test_transform.py
- regional-revenue/tests/test_transform_fx.py
- regional-revenue/tests/test_report.py
- ran `python3 -m revenue.run feed.csv` and a standalone python snippet recomputing
  per-region totals from `extract.parse_rows()` + `transform.FX_TO_USD` to verify the
  /100 and GBP hypotheses (read-only; nothing in regional-revenue/ was modified)

cannot price are not part of the total" — no warning, no count, nothing). So over half
of NA's real revenue never enters the total. Once you fix Bug A and reprice only the
priceable rows, NA comes out to $111,750.75 — dead last, exactly as last night's run
showed — but the moment GBP is priced at all (even a rough ~1.27), NA's true total
jumps to roughly $740K, comfortably above APAC's $413K and EMEA's $183K. This is why
Finance sees NA as biggest "by a wide margin" and we don't: we're quietly throwing away
its GBP orders.

**Bug C — `revenue/report.py:16`, `rank()` sorts on the wrong key.**
`transform.aggregate()` emits rows shaped `{"region_code": ..., "total_usd": ...}`
(`transform.py:25`). But `report.rank()` does:

    return sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r.get("total", 0), reverse=True)

There is no `"total"` key on real rows — only `"total_usd"` — so every row's sort key
is `0` and `sorted` (being stable) just returns the rows in whatever order
`aggregate()`'s dict produced them, i.e. first-appearance order in the feed. APAC rows
are first in `feed.csv`, so APAC "wins" by file position, not revenue. Notice
`report._amount()` two lines above (line 9-11) correctly checks `"total_usd"` first —
`rank()` and `_amount()` disagree with each other about the schema inside the same
file. So even after fixing A and B, the ranking itself is currently accidental, not
computed.

Net: the reported ranking and magnitude are both artifacts of these three bugs
compounding, and none of them are inside a single stage's "business logic" — they're
all in the undocumented/untested contract at the extract→transform and
transform→report boundaries.

## Q2

What the current 34 tests (`tests/test_extract.py`, `test_transform.py`,
`test_transform_fx.py`, `test_report.py`) verify is real, but every one of them
exercises a stage in isolation with hand-built fixtures — never the actual data shape
one stage hands the next. Concretely, it cannot catch:

- **Cross-stage schema/unit drift.** `test_transform.py`'s `rec()` helper (line 6-8)
  and `test_transform_fx.py`'s `rec()` helper (line 9-11) both pass amounts like
  `100.0` / `1000.0` directly into `transform.to_usd()`, as if they were already
  dollars. Real input from `extract.parse_rows()` is integer cents. Nothing ever pipes
  `extract`'s actual output into `transform` and checks the result, so Bug A (the
  missing /100) is invisible to this suite by construction.
- **The report.py key mismatch.** `test_report.py`'s `row()` helper (line 6-7) builds
  `{"region_code": ..., "total": ...}` — matching what `rank()` expects, not what
  `transform.aggregate()` actually produces (`"total_usd"`). The test suite for
  `report.py` was written against a schema `transform.py` doesn't emit, so it can't
  catch Bug C.
- **Silent data loss from unsupported currencies.** `test_unpriceable_currency_returns_none`
  (both transform suites) only checks that a *single record* returns `None`. Nothing
  checks what happens at the `aggregate()`/region-total level when a currency is
  missing from the rate table — there's no assertion that this is logged, counted, or
  bounded, so a whole currency silently vanishing from a region's total (Bug B) is
  unguarded.
- **No integration/golden-output test.** There is no `test_run.py` and no test that
  calls `revenue.run.main()` or chains `extract → transform → report` end to end
  against `feed.csv` (or any fixture file) with a known expected answer. All three
  bugs above only became visible when the whole pipeline was actually run against real
  data — which is exactly what none of the 34 tests do.
- **Realistic/adversarial `feed.csv` shapes.** `test_extract.py` covers dot vs comma
  decimals and one clean 3-row CSV, but not: missing/blank fields, unknown region
  strings, duplicate `order_id`s, an empty file, extra columns, or amounts with
  currency symbols.
- **Floating-point drift at scale.** `aggregate()` accumulates into a Python `float`
  (`transform.py:23-24`); no test sums enough rows, or large enough magnitudes, to
  expose accumulation error.

## Q3

No. `test_transform_fx.py` is thorough for the one thing it was scoped to — the FX
*rate table* and the conversion *arithmetic* (rate values in plausible bands, USD
identity, linearity, sign handling, zero handling) — and it would genuinely catch a
repeat of the March stale-rate incident. But of the three bugs found in Q1, it catches
zero of them:

- It never touches `report.py`, so it cannot see the `rank()` vs `"total_usd"` key
  mismatch (Bug C) — that's simply out of its file's scope.
- Its own `rec()` fixture (line 9-11) feeds `to_usd()` plain dollar-scale floats, the
  same as the older `test_transform.py`, so it inherits the same blind spot to the
  minor-units contract from `extract.py` — it cannot see Bug A.
- `test_unpriceable_currency_returns_none` (line 49-50) tests GBP specifically and
  asserts `to_usd()` returns `None` — which is *correct* given the current table, so
  it passes happily whether or not GBP is a currency you actually need to support. It
  has no test asserting `FX_TO_USD` covers every currency that appears in production
  feeds, so a real region silently losing revenue to an unpriced currency (Bug B) is
  invisible to it.

It's a good regression guard for "did someone edit a rate to the wrong number," which
was the March failure mode. It is not, and was never designed to be, a guard against
unit mismatches or missing-currency data loss — both of which are exactly what's
biting us now. We are not covered; we need an integration test against `feed.csv` (or
an equivalent fixture) with a hand-computed expected total per region, plus a test
that `FX_TO_USD` is a superset of the currencies appearing in any feed we run.
